description: Passionate about everything, had to choose something.
summary:
Sci-Tech: SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool for watching the infrared sky change over time in NASA's SPHEREx data. When a coordinate or an object name is entered, the tool:
- finds every SPHEREx exposure of that position
- reads only the pixels it needs from the open archive and masks bad pixels
- puts all exposures on one fixed sky grid
- makes one clean image per visit, in each of the six detector bands or in a wavelength window you choose

It then plays the images one after another: stars stay in place, and whatever moved or changed in brightness stands out. The tool also:
- shows the spectrum and light curve of any point you click
- marks moving and variable candidates automatically
- overlays Gaia stars moved to each visit's date, and adds the 2010 WISE image as an earlier frame
- re-measures a marked object in single exposures and exports a Minor Planet Center report draft checked against the official schema

We compared our results with published values. Marking the brown dwarf WISE 0855 in the 2010 WISE image and in the 2026 SPHEREx frame, the tool measures a motion of 8.1 ± 0.3″/yr; the published value is 8.15″/yr. From SPHEREx data alone its westward motion is 8.8 ± 1.2″/yr (published: 8.12). The candidate finder found Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B and WISE 0855 without being given their positions. The five challenge targets are prebuilt, so they work even when the server or the archive is down.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Sci-Tech: SPHEREx Blink is an open-source web tool for watching the infrared sky change over time in NASA's SPHEREx data. SPHEREx returns to each part of the sky about every six months and records it in many narrow infrared colors between 0.75 and 5 µm. Our tool takes all the images of one spot on the sky, cleans them, lines them up and plays them one after another. Stars stay still; whatever moved or changed in brightness stands out.

A user can click the sky, type a coordinate (decimal or hours-degrees) or type an object name such as "M 51". The tool then shows:

- a blink player with play/pause, speed, dated passes, arrow keys, zoom and a scale bar

- difference (one visit minus the average of the others) and sum (all visits) views

- false color from three bands

- each of the six detector bands, or any wavelength window the user drags on the spectrum

- coverage and masked-fraction maps, with saturated and low-coverage frames labeled

- Gaia DR3 stars moved to the date of each visit, and the expected track of the target

- the spectrum and light curve of any clicked point, with flag names on every point

- automatic moving and variable candidates, graded A or B

- a measuring tool for shift, direction and speed between frames

- a Minor Planet Center report draft for a marked moving object

- a context panel with AllWISE, 2MASS and DSS2 through Aladin Lite

- a share link that keeps the whole view, an embed view with embed code, and links to WiseView and IRSA

On the published site a field is 3′ or 7′ across; 15′ is available when the server is run from the repository.

The five challenge targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis) are prepared in advance and published with the page, so they work even if the server or the archive is down. For these five targets, the 2010 WISE image is added as the first frame of the blink, labeled as another instrument, together with the CatWISE2020 catalog.

Live site: https://sci-techspherex.com/

Source code: https://github.com/Ayz345/Sci-Tech-SPHEREx-Blink

HOW IT WORKS

- Image list: We built our own index of the archive. We read the pointing and the time of every SPHEREx Level 2 file in IRSA's open bucket on Amazon S3 (1,628,230 files of releases DR1 and QR3, one small range request per file), and the server finds the exposures that cover a position in that index in a few hundredths of a second, without asking IRSA's search services. Exposures newer than the index (after 5 October 2026) are asked from IRSA's SIA2 service in the background and added if it answers. The page says where each field's list came from.

- Field setup: Exposures are sorted by time and, where there is a gap longer than 30 days, split into visits. A fixed sky grid with 3″ pixels is set up, north up and east left. The grid is the same for every visit and band, which is why stars stay still in the blink. For a target with known proper motion, the grid is centered on its position at the middle of the data, and its expected position at each visit is calculated.

- Reading cutouts: SPHEREx files are about 66 MB each. Instead of downloading whole files, the server reads only the byte ranges it needs from the IMAGE, FLAGS and VARIANCE layers. This is about 2.5 MB per exposure, around 4% of the file. Every cutout is cached, so the same exposure is not read twice.

- Cleaning each exposure: Pixels with problem flags are masked, and informational flags like SOURCE are kept. A local background is removed with a sigma-clipped median, and each exposure gets a weight from its own noise.

- Resampling: Each exposure is moved onto the fixed grid with bilinear interpolation that keeps masked pixels from leaking into their neighbors. This step does not add detail; it only puts exposures taken at different rotation angles onto the same pixels.

- Combining: All exposures of one visit in one band are combined pixel by pixel with an outlier-clipped, inverse-variance weighted average. The clipping threshold has an extra term specific to SPHEREx: each exposure sees a slightly different wavelength, so a source with a steep spectrum really does change from one exposure to the next and should not be clipped. Cosmic rays, leftover bad pixels and fast asteroids are still removed.

- Saturation: "No data" and "saturated" are kept apart. Saturated pixels are drawn in the brightest color and labeled, and they are not used in difference or sum views.

- Common brightness scale: All visits in a band share one asinh scale, so the blink does not flicker because of display settings.

On top of these frames:

- Spectrum and light curve are measured from single exposures, not from the combined frames, because every exposure gives one point at its own wavelength. If a Gaia star comes within 25″ of the target, the target and its neighbors are fitted together. For R Draconis, which is saturated in every exposure, relative brightness is measured from the wings of the star's image and labeled "indicative only".

- The candidate finder subtracts a template from each visit, searches for motion by shifting and adding the visits over a grid of speeds, and fits two models to each candidate: a source moving in a straight line, and a source that changes brightness in place. Candidates explained by a known Gaia star are labeled "known". A candidate seen in two independent wavelength ranges, or detected on its own in at least 3 visits along a straight track, gets grade A; the rest get grade B. It uses no machine learning.

- For a moving object, the user marks it in at least two frames. The server finds all exposures along its path, measures its position in each single exposure, rejects bad ones with a written reason, and writes a CSV. For motion within one visit (a Solar System object) it also writes an MPC ADES draft (PSV or XML) with SPHEREx's observatory code (288) and the spacecraft position, checked against the official MPC submission schema. For a star or brown dwarf only the CSV is offered. The tool never sends anything to the Minor Planet Center; the file only goes to the user's computer.

RESULTS AND VALIDATION

- WISE 0855, the coldest known brown dwarf, is no longer at the coordinate the challenge gives: that is where it was around 2010. It is now about 2.2′ to the west. In a window we cut ourselves, 4.3–5.0 µm, it is detected in all three visits with S/N 10.9, 17.2 and 19.9.

- Marking it once in the 2010 WISE image and once in the 2026 SPHEREx frame, the tool's measuring tool gives 8.1 ± 0.3 ″/yr; the published value is 8.15. Motion measured from SPHEREx alone: −8.8 ± 1.2 and +1.5 ± 1.2 ″/yr (published: −8.12 and +0.68 ″/yr).

- Without the positions being given, the candidate finder identified WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B and Barnard's Star (grade A); it also marked RW Aurigae as variable (grade A).

- Single-exposure positions were tested against JPL Horizons on two asteroids. (433) Eros: 382 of 450 exposures accepted, median offset −0.12″ / −0.05″, scatter 0.17″ / 0.16″. (31) Euphrosyne: 275 of 350 accepted, offset −0.01″ / +0.02″.

- Our index against IRSA's own lists on the five targets: no image missing and the same file names; near the north ecliptic pole it finds about 2,000 further exposures that hold the target.

- Compared to our first prototype, background noise went down by 1.2 to 2.7 times (median 1.9) while star widths remained the same.

- On the published server, a new 7′ field shows its first band in 14–27 seconds (11 positions measured on 15 November).

- Our acceptance checklist: 102 checks passed and 6 failed, all of which were time limits on a cold start over a home connection, measured before we had our own index.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

SPHEREx data is public, but working with it is hard: the files are large, each pixel sees a different wavelength, and the archive's search services can be slow or down. Our tool removes those problems, so students, teachers and amateur astronomers can explore any region of the sky and see what changed without installing anything or writing code.

For those who want to go further, nothing is hidden: flag names, masked fractions, exposure counts, and noise and error estimates are all shown. The report draft lets users export what they measured in a form others can check.

Every view has its own shareable link and can be embedded in another web page, so teachers, museums and science writers can show specific objects. When a new SPHEREx data release comes out, it is added with one setting and one re-run of the index.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Server: Python (NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, FastAPI), running on Google Cloud Run; it can also be run locally from the repository

- Front end: plain HTML and JavaScript in the browser; the display, blink, difference, sum, false color, measuring tool and Gaia shifting are calculated on the page; three.js for the landing page

- Data: SPHEREx Level 2 images, releases DR1 and QR3, from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), read from IRSA's open Amazon S3 bucket (nasa-irsa-spherex); image lists from our own index of that bucket and from IRSA's SIA2 service

- Other data: ESA Gaia DR3, AllWISE Atlas images, CatWISE2020, CDS Sesame for name lookup, JPL Horizons for the asteroid check, the Yale Bright Star Catalogue for the stars of the sky stage

- Visualization: Aladin Lite (AllWISE, 2MASS, DSS2)

- Standards: MPC ADES 2022 format, checked against the official submit.xsd schema

- Index build: GitHub Actions, 20 parallel jobs of about a minute each

- License: MIT

USE OF AI

We received assistance from Claude Code (Anthropic) for the code, tests and documentation, under the team's direction; the team chose the challenge, the goals, the features and the claims. Every commit in the repository carries a "Co-Authored-By: Claude" line. The 3D spacecraft model on the landing page is AI-generated (3D Jutsu) and labeled wherever it appears. No sky image, frame, spectrum or number is AI-generated or AI-enhanced, and the candidate finder is a classical algorithm, not machine learning. The background music of the demo video is AI-generated (Eleven Music, made through Higgsfield) and its narration is an AI-generated stock voice (ElevenLabs text-to-speech through Higgsfield; no human voice, no voice cloning), as stated on its last card; its sound effects are synthesized in code.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- Instead of downloading 66 MB files, we read only the bytes we need from the open S3 bucket. This makes it possible to open any coordinate live.

- When the archive's search services went down on the last day, we indexed the archive ourselves from the headers of its 1.6 million files, so the tool no longer waits for them.

- SPHEREx sees each pixel at a different wavelength. We use that: users can choose their own wavelength window, and our combining step was changed so it does not throw away real changes caused by a source's spectrum.

- Adding the 2010 WISE image as the first frame turns a year of SPHEREx data into a 16-year baseline.

- Gaia stars are moved to the date of each visit, so users can see where a star should be and check that the tool agrees.

- A space telescope's data is turned into a report draft in the format astronomers use for the Minor Planet Center, including the spacecraft's position.

- R Draconis is too bright for normal measurements, so we measure it from the wings of its image instead.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Archive speed and outages: We measured three ways of finding images through IRSA's services. SIA2 took around 3.3 seconds, TAP between 77 and 174 seconds, and resolving file addresses through DataLink 70–80 seconds per file. We first chose SIA2. On the first evening it returned errors for about two thirds of requests, and on the last day it was down for hours, so no new position could be opened. We then built our own index from the files in IRSA's open bucket; the image list and the pixels now both come from that bucket.

- Working without the server: The five challenge targets are prepared in advance and work even if the server and the archive are down.

- Wavelength mixing: Each exposure in a visit sees a different wavelength, which could create fake brightness changes. Our bands and windows only use exposures whose wavelength at the target is inside the chosen range.

- Honesty about limits: We list what the tool cannot do (below). The candidate list shows places to look, not discoveries. Errors that we measured to be too small are labeled on the page.

- Safety in reports: The report draft never sends data anywhere.

- Protecting the server: requests are rate-limited so that one visitor cannot block the others.

KNOWN LIMITS

- SPHEREx pixels are 6.15″. Our 3″ grid and the zoom on the page do not add detail, and we do not use deconvolution or AI sharpening.

- Bright stars leave small black-and-white pairs in difference images.

- Bright extended objects (M31, the Orion Nebula) in the shortest band: SPHEREx flags most of each exposure's pixels there as crosstalk and we leave flagged pixels out, so large parts of a frame can be empty or shown as saturated. The second and longer bands are much less affected. The tool was built and tested on point sources.

- The candidate finder usually misses objects that move less than about 10″ over the data, and it is less sensitive in crowded fields. In a test with artificial sources placed in the data, it found 83% of sources moving 9″ and 100% of those moving 15″ in sparse fields, but only 44% at 15″ in crowded fields.

- R Draconis is saturated in every exposure, so the candidate finder cannot find it, and its brightness change is shown only as indicative.

- Exposure times have not been independently verified, and one of the two test asteroids (Eros) shows an unexplained offset of about 0.15″ along its track.

- Our index ends with the exposure of 5 October 2026; later exposures appear only if IRSA's SIA2 service answers.

- Opening a new coordinate depends on IRSA's open S3 bucket and on our server, which can be busy when several fields are built at once. The gallery always works.

- Gaia stars depend on ESA's archive service; when it does not answer, the page says so and the images and spectra work without them.

- WISE images and the CatWISE catalog are only available for the five gallery targets.

DATA AND ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS

- NASA: SPHEREx Level 2 images (DR1, QR3) and the SPHEREx Explanatory Supplement, AllWISE Atlas images and the CatWISE2020 catalog, all from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA); JPL Horizons.

- ESA: Gaia DR3.

- CDS, Strasbourg: Sesame name resolver and Aladin Lite (LGPL v3).

- Yale Bright Star Catalogue, 5th revised edition (Hoffleit & Warren 1991), for the stars of the sky stage.

- WiseView (byw.tools/wiseview), named by the challenge: the player is modelled on it.

- Minor Planet Center: observatory codes and the IAU ADES format and schema.

- Luhman & Esplin (2016) for the motion of WISE 0855; Eisenhardt et al. (2020) and Marocco et al. (2021) for CatWISE.

- Software: Python, NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX, PyVO, Requests, lxml, pytest; three.js; fonts from Google Fonts (SIL Open Font License); coastlines from Natural Earth.

- Full list with licenses: the README of the repository. Our code is under the MIT license.
